corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The framework is purely allocative: with no market clearing (zero demand or no institutional venue) personal information has no price and the entire mechanism collapses to the pre-market default of uncompensated collection â€” the model says nothing about the information's residual sensitivity, only that its market value is zero.
corpus.novelty_claim: Personal information should be a market-alienable property right traded through a National Information Market so individuals share in the revenue from their data.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Shares the core propertization move â€” the subject owns their personal data as capital and should capture surplus from its use rather than have it extracted for free â€” and both frame privacy in explicit market-pricing terms rather than as cost or PIA-style subject harm, positing an institutional venue (Laudon's National Information Market / information-market intermediaries; PVM's consent-interface bargaining under IEEE 7012) that moves the subject's share off a near-zero floor.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Laudon's unit is the named subject's tradeable record priced by market demand (single scalar), with ownership made ALIENABLE by design (you sell it) and no adversary, horizon, or reconstruction bound; PVM instead makes the object a system property â€” a per-subject reconstruction bound R(t) gated by a mechanism property Phi â€” makes inalienability STRUCTURAL (non-reconstruction) rather than a market of licensable copies, treats durability as finite and adversary-relative, and locates the observer/subject gap in market-position RENT (atomisation + venue exclusion) explicitly rejecting the raw-record aggregation/compounding that Laudon's per-record pricing presumes.
corpus.citation: Kenneth C. Laudon, "Markets and Privacy," Communications of the ACM, Vol. 39, No. 9 (September 1996), pp. 92â€“104.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The paper offers no quantitative metric, so there is no numeric axis to zero out; its qualitative claim instead identifies the opposite failure â€” when the market/alienability axis is fully present, free transferability defeats the privacy the property right was meant to secure.
corpus.novelty_claim: Granting individuals a property (IP-style) right in their personal data is unlikely to achieve privacy goals because property law's default favors free alienability, so once licensed the data flows onward unchecked (paraphrase of Samuelson's thesis, not a verbatim quote).
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both treat a person's data as a potential asset owned by the subject (subject-owned capital / propertization) and both make alienability the central design question; Samuelson analyzes exactly the market-for-personal-data / consent-licensing model that PVM's consent-interface bargaining game also assumes, and both accept that a naive property market pushes the subject's realized share toward a near-zero, weakly-protected floor.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Samuelson's object is the named subject's impact under legal-construction rights with no system property, no reconstruction bound R(t), no finite adversary-relative horizon, and no equilibrium bargaining/pricing formalism â€” she frames the market only to reject propertization. PVM answers her core alienability objection structurally: inalienability comes from information-theoretic non-reconstruction rather than legal construction, the unit of analysis is a system property (Phi-gated R) not after-the-fact subject harm, and the observer-subject gap is modeled as market-position rent corrected by a published propose-and-respond standard (IEEE 7012), none of which Samuelson entertains.
corpus.citation: Pamela Samuelson, "Privacy As Intellectual Property?", 52 Stanford Law Review 1125-1173 (2000).

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The regime attaches only to information that is both "personal" and market-tradable, so if either axis is absent (data is non-identifiable, or there is no commercial trade) the propertization model has no asset to protect and simply does not engage.
corpus.novelty_claim: Personal data should be propertized but bounded by a five-element "hybrid inalienability" regime (use-transfer restrictions, opt-in defaults, right of exit, damages, and market-policing institutions) that preserves a data market while protecting privacy.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both assign ownership of personal data to the subject (subject-owned capital / propertization) and both treat inalienability as the central safeguard preventing full commodification, rather than allowing free outright sale; both accept that a market for the asset exists and that the subject's default position is weak and must be corrected.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Schwartz's inalienability is a LEGAL construction (a Calabresi-Melamed hybrid rule enforced by statute and institutions), whereas PVM makes inalienability STRUCTURAL via an information-theoretic non-reconstruction bound; Schwartz's unit is the named subject's normative interest, not a system property Phi gating a per-subject reconstruction bound R(t); he has no finite adversary-relative durability horizon, no subgame-perfect bargaining-game equilibrium for the subject's surplus share, and no rent-vs-aggregation decomposition of the observer-subject value gap â€” his economics is qualitative market-failure/commodification reasoning, not formal market pricing of a surplus split.
corpus.citation: Paul M. Schwartz, Property, Privacy, and Personal Data, 117 Harv. L. Rev. 2056 (2004).

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: Without a tradeable/commodified object the "individual control" claim has no enforceable referent and collapses; Purtova further argues that after the Big Data turn the per-subject property metric is already ill-defined because value and harm are relational (spillover/network effects across many subjects), so the individual-ownership axis is effectively zero even when nominally present.
corpus.novelty_claim: Paraphrase (not a verified direct quote): enforceable individual property rights in personal data no longer make sense after the Big Data turn, because data's relational, spillover, and network-effect character defeats individual control and transparency.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Shares PVM's core propertization move: treating personal data as an asset whose ownership could be assigned to the subject (subject-owned capital), and directly engages the commodification/alienability question PVM inherits. Both also reject naive per-record individual control as insufficient at scale, and Purtova's emphasis that data value is relational and spills across subjects echoes PVM's rejection of raw-record compounding as the source of the observer-subject gap.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Purtova's framing is doctrinal-legal: inalienability and control are matters of legal construction, and she ultimately concludes property rights FAIL after Big Data, offering no pricing mechanism. PVM instead (a) makes inalienability STRUCTURAL via an information-theoretic non-reconstruction bound R(t) rather than legal construction, (b) supplies an explicit market-pricing engine (subgame-perfect equilibrium of a consent-interface bargaining game, IEEE 7012 propose-and-respond moving the subject's surplus share off the floor), (c) locates the observer-subject gap in market-position RENT (atomisation discount, exclusion from the clearing venue) rather than in Purtova's relational spillover/network-effect account, and (d) reframes durability as a finite, adversary-relative horizon rather than a static legal entitlement. Purtova's relational-failure argument is closer to a reason property fails than PVM's proposed remedy, so it does not pre-empt PVM's mechanism.
corpus.citation: Nadezhda Purtova, "The illusion of personal data as no one's property," Law, Innovation and Technology 7(1) (2015): 83-111; see also N. Purtova, Property Rights in Personal Data: A European Perspective (Kluwer Law International, 2011/2012) and "Do Property Rights in Personal Data Make Sense after the Big Data Turn? Individual Control and Transparency" (2017).

corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Prins is normative legal doctrine over a named subject's data, not a system property; no information-theoretic reconstruction bound R(t), no finite adversary-relative horizon, no bargaining game / subgame-perfect surplus share, and no market-position-rent vs super-additive-aggregation distinction. Critically, she debates inalienability as a matter of legal construction, whereas PVM makes inalienability STRUCTURAL (non-reconstruction), and she offers no adversary model or pricing mechanism, only whether a property right ought to exist.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The paper carries no quantitative metric, so it does not "go to zero"; its normative case simply collapses when the bargaining-asymmetry axis is set to zero â€” if atomised individuals already had adequate bargaining power, the rationale for fiduciary intermediation would evaporate.
corpus.novelty_claim: Bottom-up fiduciary data trusts â€” an ecology of trustee-governed arrangements subjects can choose among and defect from â€” as an alternative to both one-size-fits-all governance and individual data ownership.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Shares PVM's core diagnosis that atomised individuals hold near-zero bargaining position against data collectors and that the remedy is POOLED bargaining leverage rather than individual action; both reject naive individual propertization as sufficient and locate the value deficit in market/negotiating position rather than in raw record volume.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Its object is an institutional-legal governance mechanism (the fiduciary trust), not a system property; PVM's unit is a quantitative, information-theoretic reconstruction bound R(t) gated by Phi, with no analogue here (no finite adversary-relative horizon). PVM prices the surplus share as a subgame-perfect equilibrium of a consent-interface bargaining game (market_pricing) and keeps a published-standard proposer inversion; Delacroix-Lawrence stays at the incentive/governance level with no equilibrium pricing. Most sharply, PVM assigns ownership to the SUBJECT (subject-owned capital with structural inalienability), whereas this paper deliberately routes rights AWAY from individual ownership into a trustee-held intermediary â€” the opposite locus of control.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: If a data contribution's marginal productive value is zero, the data-as-labor claim degenerates: there is no wage to pay and the entire compensation/redistribution argument collapses to the "free" baseline it opposes, since value is defined purely by market productivity with no information-theoretic floor.
corpus.novelty_claim: Reconceive user data as labor to be compensated rather than as free capital, restoring a functioning market for individual data contributions.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both reject the default that data is free capital passively observed by firms and instead vest value/ownership in the SUBJECT (propertization); both diagnose the observer-to-subject gap as a MARKET-POSITION problem â€” their data monopsony maps onto PVM's atomisation discount and exclusion from the clearing venue â€” and both prescribe a pooled/intermediated bargaining remedy: their mediators of individual data (MIDs) are functionally PVM's pooled bargaining position, and both aim to move the subject's surplus share off a near-zero floor via changed market structure rather than replicated scale.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: The unit of analysis is the individual contributor's economic welfare/wage (subject_impact), not a system property; there is no per-subject reconstruction bound R, no gating property Phi, and no finite adversary-relative horizon â€” data value is a durable labor-productivity quantity with no information-theoretic drift. Economic framing is a labor/monopsony market with collective bargaining, not a subgame-perfect equilibrium of a specified consent-interface game anchored to a published proposer-inverting standard (IEEE 7012). Inalienability is legal/market-constructed (property + unions) rather than structural non-reconstruction, and the paper does not frame the value gap as super-additive-aggregation-vs-rent nor cite returns-to-scale evidence to reject raw-record compounding â€” it leaves aggregate data value largely as a productivity primitive.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: Value is the marginal product of the individual's data in a labor market, so when firm demand or the data's marginal contribution is absent (redundant/substitutable data), the imputed wage collapses to zero and the person is owed nothing â€” the metric has no floor independent of a counterparty.
corpus.novelty_claim: Treat personal data as compensated labor rather than as free capital, and let individuals collectively bargain (data labor unions) for its market value.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both locate economic value in the individual's data and argue the subject should capture surplus currently taken by platforms; both invoke pooled/collective bargaining (data labor unions ~ PVM's pooled bargaining position) to lift the subject's share off a near-zero atomised floor; both reject naive per-record scaling by noting individual data has low standalone/marginal value.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Opposite on the capital/labor axis: Radical Markets explicitly argues data is LABOR (a wage flow), whereas PVM treats it as subject-owned CAPITAL with a finite, adversary-relative durability horizon. Its unit is subject_impact (worker compensation) with no system property; PVM anchors value in an information-theoretic reconstruction bound R(t), a system property with an explicit adversary â€” both absent here. It explains low individual value via monopsony/marginal-product economics, not market-position rent from exclusion at a clearing venue, and offers no consent-interface bargaining game, no subgame-perfect equilibrium, no IEEE 7012 proposer inversion, and no structural (non-reconstruction) inalienability â€” its data-labor is alienable and tradeable.

corpus.paper_id: Acquisti, Taylor, Wagman 2016 â€” The Economics of Privacy (JEL 54(2):442â€“492)
corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: Because the paper's central result is that privacy's welfare effect is sign-ambiguous and context/aggregation-dependent, zeroing or removing an input axis leaves the claim indeterminate â€” it yields no scalar bound or directional prediction, only "it depends."
corpus.novelty_claim: Paraphrased (survey, not a single quoted thesis): synthesizes diverse theoretical and empirical streams to show privacy involves economic trade-offs whose costs and benefits are context- and aggregation-dependent, so protection vs. disclosure has no unambiguous welfare sign.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both treat personal information as economically valuable and both foreground that its value is aggregation- and context-sensitive; ATW's discussion of returns to data, the observer/firm capturing consumer surplus, and value arising from combination directly touches PVM's observer-to-subject gap and its interrogation of returns-to-scale in raw records.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: ATW frames privacy as an ex-post welfare trade-off between named parties (consumers vs. firms) measured as an ambiguous scalar, with no system-property unit. It has no information-theoretic reconstruction bound R(t), no finite adversary-relative horizon, no consent-interface bargaining subgame with a subject surplus-share equilibrium, no reclassification of the value gap as market-position rent vs. super-additive aggregation, and no structural (non-reconstruction) inalienability or subject-owned propertization; it surveys these debates rather than pricing the subject's share as an SPE.
corpus.citation: Acquisti, Alessandro, Curtis Taylor, and Liad Wagman. 2016. "The Economics of Privacy." Journal of Economic Literature 54 (2): 442â€“492.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The metric is a single elicited money amount (WTA or WTP) for one named subject's own data, so with no adversary or system axis at all it still returns a finite dollar figure â€” but that figure is framing-dependent and non-unique (WTA roughly 5x WTP), so the "value of privacy" is undefined as a stable scalar rather than degenerating to zero.
corpus.novelty_claim: Privacy valuations are not stable: they flip with endowment (WTA vs WTP) and question order, so people value the same data 5x differently.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both treat privacy as a priceable economic quantity rather than a cost or a compliance checkbox, and both locate the observer/subject value gap as a wedge to be explained rather than assumed; Acquisti et al.'s WTA/WTP endowment gap is direct empirical evidence that the subject's realized price sits far below any stable "true" valuation and is highly sensitive to the interface/framing that elicits it â€” which is exactly the near-zero-floor-and-framing-dependence premise PVM builds its consent-interface bargaining game on top of.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: Its unit of analysis is the impact/experience of a named subject (a survey-elicited stated valuation, ISO/PIA-adjacent), whereas PVM's unit is a system property â€” a reconstruction bound R gated by Phi; its "market pricing" is descriptive elicitation of individual preferences, not a subgame-perfect equilibrium of a bargaining game moved by a published standard (IEEE 7012); it has no adversary, no finite adversary-relative durability horizon R(t), no returns-to-scale/aggregation argument, and it treats the observer-subject gap as a cognitive/framing artifact (endowment, order effects) rather than as structural market-position rent (atomisation discount + venue exclusion). It also makes no propertization or structural-inalienability claim.
corpus.citation: Acquisti, A., John, L. K., & Loewenstein, G. (2013). What Is Privacy Worth? The Journal of Legal Studies, 42(2), 249â€“274.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: When the information axis is absent (respondent uninformed about what their data is/does), the elicited WTA does not converge: it becomes highly dispersed and bimodal and systematically depressed for low-information groups, so the scalar is friction-driven rather than a stable value.
corpus.novelty_claim: Information frictions cause dispersed, heterogeneous personal-data valuations; an information treatment revises valuations upward, concentrated among low-valuation individuals.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both attach a dollar figure to a subject's personal data and both diagnose that the subject's floor valuation is low, dispersed, and demographically stratified; both are motivated by redistributing data value back to subjects and by explaining why subjects appear to under-price their own data (their frictions vs PVM's atomisation).
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: The paper measures a named subject's self-reported WTA after the fact (subject_impact, single dollar scalar) via incentive-compatible elicitation, with no adversary and no reconstruction bound; PVM instead defines value as a SYSTEM property â€” a per-subject reconstruction bound R(t) gated by Phi over a finite, adversary-relative horizon â€” prices the subject's share as a subgame-perfect bargaining equilibrium under IEEE 7012 propose-and-respond, and reads the observer-subject gap as market-position rent (atomisation/venue-exclusion), not as an information-friction or preference artifact; where this paper treats low valuations as correctable misperception, PVM treats them as structural rent extraction.

Information Frictions and Heterogeneity in Valuations of Personal Data. 21st Workshop on the Economics of Information Security (WEIS 2022). Median WTA to share entirety of Facebook data = $750 (YouGov nationally representative sample); $1,000 (Data Dividend Project sample); bimodal distribution clustered below $250 and above $10,000.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The headline result is a revealed price elasticity: when the price differential axis goes to zero (identical prices), the willingness-to-pay signal collapses to indifference (subjects split evenly between shops), so the metric measures the price wedge, not any intrinsic privacy valuation, and yields nothing when price is absent.
corpus.novelty_claim: When a store charging less requests more personal data, almost all buyers pick it despite stating strong privacy preferences (a ~1-euro discount reverses professed intent).
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both treat privacy as a priced market quantity settled at a transaction, and both locate the subject's realized privacy value far below their stated/latent value â€” PVM's "near-zero floor" is empirically this paper's revealed unwillingness to pay a 1-euro premium.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: This measures after-the-fact behavioral impact on named human subjects (a WTP field experiment), not a system property; it has no reconstruction bound R(t), no adversary, no finite-horizon durable asset, no bargaining-game equilibrium, and no propertization/ownership claim â€” the low value is an observed demand fact, whereas PVM diagnoses the same floor as structural market-position rent to be moved by inverting the proposer role via a consent-interface standard.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The elicited price is a single stated-preference scalar per subject, so if the subject reports zero valuation (or declines to protect at any positive price) the metric collapses to "privacy is worth nothing" with no residual structural quantity to fall back on â€” value is defined only by revealed money-vs-data choice.
corpus.novelty_claim: Subjects overwhelmingly prefer even trivial money (as little as 25 cents) over protecting or withholding their personal data, and exhibit a large WTP-to-protect vs WTA-to-sell gap.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both treat privacy as an economically priced quantity rather than a compliance harm, both put a monetary figure on a subject's personal information, and both engage the subject as the party whose data carries the value (subject-side valuation / subject-owned asset intuition).

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: The paper offers no single formal metric, so when the privacy or value axis is absent its market-failure claims degrade to qualitative narrative rather than producing an undefined or degenerate number.
corpus.novelty_claim: Agenda-setting survey structuring the economic, technical, social and ethical frictions (asymmetric information, externalities, uncertain valuation) that make personal-data markets and privacy hard to reconcile.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Shares the premise that personal data is a tradable economic asset whose valuation is hard and whose markets systematically fail, and both observe that data collectors capture value individuals do not (the observer-to-subject gap); both frame the problem through market pricing rather than pure cost.
corpus.divergence_from_pvm: This is a qualitative multi-issue survey with no formal metric: it has no system-property reconstruction bound R(t), no subgame-perfect consent-bargaining game, no IEEE 7012 propose-and-respond mechanism, no finite adversary-relative durability horizon, and no structural (non-reconstruction) inalienability; it catalogs why markets fail rather than proposing a mechanism that repositions the subject's surplus share, and it attributes the value gap to generic market frictions rather than PVM's specific market-position rent (atomisation discount plus exclusion from the clearing venue).

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: If the incentive/strategic axis is removed (assume all parties' incentives aligned), the explanatory claim collapses to nothing â€” security reduces to a purely technical problem and the paper's entire thesis has no content, since the metric is the misalignment itself.
corpus.novelty_claim: Information insecurity stems as much from perverse economic incentives as from technical factors.
corpus.overlap_with_pvm: Both locate value/failure in economic structure rather than raw technical mechanism, and both invoke an asymmetric-information market failure: Anderson's Akerlof-lemons argument (good security can't command a price premium because buyers cannot verify quality) is the same lineage PVM leans on for its atomisation-discount / market-position-rent claim, where the subject cannot price or clear their data at fair value. His lemons story is about unverifiable product quality, whereas PVM's gap is specifically atomisation plus exclusion from the clearing venue â€” a redistribution-of-bargaining-position mechanism Anderson does not model. PVM should not claim novelty over Anderson on 'economics matters for security'; its novelty is the per-subject system-property metric and the pricing/bargaining mechanism, not the general incentive insight.

corpus.failure_mode_on_missing_axis: There is no economic axis to zero out; on the mechanism axis, as epsilon grows without bound the guarantee degenerates to no protection (the multiplicative bound e^epsilon becomes vacuous), while epsilon to 0 forces the output distribution to ignore the data entirely and destroys utility.

verdict.rationale: The claim's stated positive content -- shifting the unit of analysis from after-the-fact, named-subject impact (ISO/PIA) to an ex-ante, architectural system property that bounds an adversary's per-subject reconstruction -- is anticipated. The delegator supplies covering prior art for each half of the move and, critically, for the exact contrast the claim rests on: (1) the system-property/reconstruction-bound structure R-gated-by-Phi is the founding form of QIF (Smith 2009 min-entropy vulnerability IS a per-secret one-guess reconstruction bound; the channel/mechanism gates it) and DP (Dwork 2006 epsilon IS an ex-ante mechanism property gating disclosure, Dinur-Nissim 2003 the per-record reconstruction threshold); and (2) Wagner & Boiten 2018 ("From Art to Science, By Metrics") explicitly argues the PIA tradition should be replaced by quantified system-level metrics -- the same subject-survey-to-system-metric transition the claim names as its novelty. The prover already concedes the reconstruction-bound object is not novel (Balle/DP own it) and retreats to a BRIDGE: installing that object as the *unit a PIA is conducted over*, plus a two-level Phi-vs-R separation. But QIF/DP already carry the two-level structure (channel vs vulnerability; epsilon vs reconstruction bound), and Wagner & Boiten already relocate quantified adversary/system metrics into the risk-assessment slot. What remains is a re-contextualization (apply an existing QIF/DP object as the assessment unit), which a competent reader combining the two named traditions reaches without invention. The prover's defense that Wagner & Boiten "keeps the unit as subject-impact" is only partly true and does not rescue the claim, because the mechanism-property-as-unit half is then simply supplied by QIF/DP -- so no single feature of the bridge is un-anticipated. On the claim's own stated scope (unit-of-analysis shift, economics explicitly excluded), it is anticipated. Hard-marker call: MIRAGE.
verdict.residual_novel_core: The tightest thing that survives is a packaging/framing move, not a new object: explicitly positioning a governance-facing, independently verifiable mechanism property Phi -- held two-level-distinct from the per-subject reconstruction bound R it gates -- as the single unit that a privacy impact-assessment/valuation instrument is conducted over. No one cited work states this exact assembly verbatim (QIF/DP have the object but not the PIA-instrument framing; Wagner-Boiten has the PIA-to-metric framing but does not name Phi-gates-R as the unit). But this residual is a re-contextualization of the QIF/DP object into the PIA-unit slot, obvious in light of the two named traditions, and too thin to carry CTR-LR-01 as written. Its only genuinely un-verbatim element is the deliberate Phi/R governance-vs-quantity separation offered as the assessment unit.

prove.strongest_form: Scoped to the privacy impact-assessment / governance tradition: PVM is the first to make the *unit of assessment itself* an ex-ante mechanism property Phi that gates a per-subject reconstruction bound R, in place of the tradition's after-the-fact subject-impact object (likelihood x severity to a named individual, ISO/IEC 29134 / 29100). The defensible move is a BRIDGE, not the reconstruction bound per se: it imports the system-property, adversary-relative reconstruction-bound stance from the QIF/DP line and installs it as the assessment/valuation unit that a PIA is conducted over. The claim is NOT that R-gated-by-Phi is a new information-theoretic object (it is not), but that (a) the unit of analysis in an impact/governance instrument moves from subject-impact to a verifiable system property, and (b) Phi (the architected/checkable mechanism property) is held distinct from R (the per-subject disclosure quantity it delivers) â€” a two-level separation that neither the PIA tradition nor the flat leakage-metric tradition draws.
prove.why_novel: The two neighbouring traditions each hold exactly one of the claim's two features and never both. (1) The quantified-PIA / de-identification-risk line (El Emam, Health Canada re-identification thresholds, EBIOS-style ability x impact, CSIRO R4) already made the PIA ex-ante and quantitative â€” but its unit stayed subject-impact: the metric is a named individual's re-identification probability / expected number of re-identifications, a statistical property of a released dataset scored by ability-times-impact-to-the-subject, not a mechanism property Phi. It quantifies subject risk; it does not shift the unit off the subject. (2) The reconstruction-bound line (Dwork 2006 epsilon; Smith 2009 min-entropy vulnerability = one-guess reconstruction; Balle et al. 2022 informed-adversary reconstruction bounds under DP) delivers the system-property object â€” a per-record/per-subject reconstruction bound gated by a mechanism property â€” but only as a security-analysis, auditing, or attack-success metric; none frames that object as the unit of a privacy impact assessment / governance instrument, and none separates a governance-facing mechanism property Phi from the per-subject bound R it gates and positions Phi as what the assessment is conducted over. PVM's novelty is precisely the un-occupied intersection: relocating the reconstruction-bound/system-property stance into the assessment-and-valuation unit-of-analysis, thereby answering the PIA question ("what is the privacy impact?") with an architectural, ex-ante, verifiable system property rather than an after-the-fact subject survey â€” and doing so with the Phi-gates-R two-level structure. Against the ISO/PIA foil the win is clean and uncontested; the surviving novelty against the strongest challengers is this bridge, not the bound.
prove.load_bearing_prior_it_must_beat: Balle, Cherubin & Hayes, "Reconstructing Training Data with Informed Adversaries" (IEEE S&P 2022, arXiv:2201.04845) â€” the DP reconstruction-bound line (with Dwork 2006 and Smith 2009 min-entropy vulnerability as the in-corpus proxies). It is the closest because it most nearly instantiates the claim's literal technical core: a per-subject reconstruction-success bound gated by a mechanism/system property. The claim survives it ONLY in scoped form â€” PVM must not claim novelty on the reconstruction-bound object itself (Balle/DP already own it), but on installing that object as the unit of analysis of privacy impact assessment/valuation, a framing Balle never makes (it audits/attacks a mechanism, it does not assess, govern, or value the subject's position). The secondary prior it must survive is the quantified re-identification-risk-assessment tradition (El Emam / EBIOS / Health Canada thresholds), which shares the ex-ante, assessment-embedded framing but keeps the unit as subject-impact rather than a mechanism property.

prove.strongest_form: Reading the consent interface itself as the extensive form of one named non-cooperative bargaining game (Rubinstein 1982 alternating offers), the subject-side near-zero surplus share is DERIVED, not asserted or measured, as the unique subgame-perfect share of the ultimatum restriction where the counterparty is sole proposer: s = h_X, with h_X approximately 0 because the subject is excluded from the clearing venue. The same one model then yields a proved comparative static: inverting the proposer identity, exactly the inversion a published standard (IEEE 7012 propose-and-respond) performs, moves the SPE share off the floor to an interior value s = beta in (0,1). The novel object is the interface-as-extensive-form generator of the share (who-proposes and how-many-rounds fixes the equilibrium split), not the empirical fact that the share is small nor the normative claim that individual-proposed terms empower the subject. Deliberately NOT claimed as novel: that behavioural data is undervalued; that notice-and-consent is rhetorically take-it-or-leave-it; that Rubinstein bargaining can be applied to data pricing in general; that IEEE 7012 shifts bargaining power.
prove.why_novel: The corpus splits into two families and the claim slots into the gap between them. verdict.rationale: The strongest form of CTR-LR-04 decomposes into three planks, and the delegator produced substantial, corpus-internal prior art for each â€” plus works that already fuse them. (1) "Gap = market-position rent, not subject productivity": Bergemann-Bonatti-Gan (2022) formally derives the aggregator capturing the total information value while atomised individuals capture almost nothing, driven by the social-data externality and price-collapsing competition among sellers â€” i.e., the gap framed as structural market position, not super-additive productivity accruing to the subject. Posner-Weyl/Arrieta-Ibarra locate low individual value in monopsony (a bargaining/position rent, explicitly not intrinsic productivity). Atomised sellers facing a concentrated buyer with no competitive clearing venue simply IS monopsony; "atomisation discount + exclusion from the clearing venue" is a relabeling, not a new mechanism. (2) "Returns-to-scale rejects raw-record compounding": supplied directly by Bajari-Chernozhukov-Hortacsu-Suzuki (2019) flat-N / diminishing-T findings and by the Arnold-Marcus / "data is not the new oil" line. (3) "Pool bargaining position, not scale": this is verbatim the standing data-union / data-consortia program (arXiv:2506.10272, 1906.11803, the CalLawRev data-unions piece). The claim explicitly concedes the two ideas it does not own ("structure suppresses value" and "pool for leverage") and rests novelty on the JOINT move; but the joint move is closely anticipated by combining works already co-present in the corpus, several of which (Bergemann-Bonatti-Gan; the data-union papers) themselves bundle rent-framing with either scale-capture or position-pooling. Under D2, the absence of a single verbatim "rent vs super-additive aggregation" corrective is not novelty when the components are independently and jointly covered. Hard-marker call: substantially covered â†’ MIRAGE.
verdict.residual_novel_core: What the delegator did NOT surface as an explicit, stated argument is the directed INTERNAL critique of the data-as-labour prescription: using the flat-N returns-to-scale evidence to deny that a positive marginal product of an additional raw record exists, thereby showing that data-as-labour's "raise the wage toward marginal product via a labour cartel" remedy self-defeats (marginal product â‰ˆ 0), and re-specifying the redistributive object as venue-access/clearing-position rent rather than a wage. Bergemann-Bonatti-Gan derives the structural gap but does not aim it as a refutation of the productivity premise; Bajari supplies the elasticity but does not turn it against the labour framing. The tightest surviving claim is therefore this narrow, evidenced falsifier â€” "scale-replication data cooperatives fail because returns-to-scale are flat, so only pooling venue/bargaining position redistributes" â€” stated as a directed correction to the labour-union/propertization program inside a reconstruction-bound / IEEE-7012 frame. The broad rent-not-aggregation diagnosis and the pool-position prescription do not survive.

prove.strongest_form: The observer-to-subject data-value gap is MARKET-POSITION RENT â€” an atomisation discount plus exclusion from the clearing venue â€” and NOT super-additive aggregation value; returns-to-scale evidence (diminishing/non-compounding marginal value of additional raw records) rejects raw-record compounding as the source of the gap. The load-bearing, defensible novelty is the joint move: (a) an EVIDENCED decomposition that severs the aggregate's value from raw-record compounding and reassigns the residual to position rent, which directly contradicts the field's superadditive-aggregation consensus; and (b) the resulting prescriptive correction â€” redistribution requires pooling BARGAINING POSITION (venue access), NOT replicating aggregation SCALE â€” which predicts that scale-replication data cooperatives fail precisely because scale is not where the value sits. The claim does NOT assert novelty on 'market structure suppresses individual data value' or on 'pool to gain leverage'; those are conceded to the data-as-labour school. Its novelty is the returns-to-scale-grounded rent-vs-aggregation decomposition and the consequent re-specification of WHAT is pooled.
prove.why_novel: The dominant view in the personal-data-economics literature is the OPPOSITE of this claim's premise: Galperti-Levkun-Perego ('The Value of Data Records', ReStud) and the 'synergistic/superadditive value of information' tradition hold that individual records are near-worthless in isolation but generate surplus through superadditive combination â€” i.e., the gap IS genuine aggregation value. CTR-LR-04 rejects this by marshalling returns-to-scale evidence (Varian's 'data barrier to entry', ML data-scaling curves showing sub-proportional, diminishing marginal value of additional records) to argue raw records do not compound super-additively, so the residual gap is rent, not synergy. The closest remedial competitor â€” the data-as-labour/monopsony school (Posner-Weyl 2018; Arrieta-Ibarra et al. 2018) â€” also diagnoses low individual value structurally and prescribes pooling, but it treats aggregate data value as a genuine PRODUCTIVITY primitive (data is labour that produces value; workers are simply underpaid relative to marginal product under monopsony) and its 'pool' is a wage-raising labour cartel. It never severs aggregate value from raw-record compounding, never uses returns-to-scale evidence to deny the productivity premise, and therefore never distinguishes pooling-for-scale from pooling-for-position. CTR-LR-04's diagnosis changes the OBJECT of redistribution: because the value is position rent rather than compounded productivity, pooling to replicate the platform's aggregation scale is futile, and only pooling bargaining position / venue access moves the subject's share â€” a falsifiable prediction the labour-union prescription does not make. This is a specific, evidenced correction to the data-as-labour / propertization thin-markets premise, not a restatement of it.

Mosca does not merely assert an abstract adversary-relative horizon; it joins the drifting-adversary horizon to a required-protection TERM (X), which is exactly the 'convert-drift-into-a-maturity' move the prover claims is unclaimed. The prover leans on 'upward-drift-with-adversary' (ingredients 2/3) as the engine that distinguishes PVM from staleness-based depreciation â€” but that engine, tied to a term, is precisely Mosca. The load-bearing prior the prover picked to beat (staleness-clock data depreciation) is the wrong threat; Mosca is the real covering art and pre-empts the structural core, not just the 'finite durability per se' concession. What genuinely survives is narrower than the claim as stated: Mosca prices/propertizes nothing (a confidentiality risk-planning heuristic, not a capital-asset valuation) and its clock is a computational-cryptographic break-time, not an information-theoretic reconstruction bound in the Dinur-Nissim/QIF sense. Concession that keeps it defensible: finite durability of a data asset per se is NOT claimed novel â€” only that the term is a function of a drifting reconstruction bound. So the tight claim is: no propertization or data-valuation work sets an asset's durability as f(R(t)) where R(t) is an adversary-relative reconstruction bound.

(1) Data-depreciation/half-life valuation has a finite term but drives it by endogenous staleness (relevance decay, a fixed accounting factor over elapsed time); PVM's term is driven by an EXOGENOUS, adversary-relative reconstruction bound and can move independently of â€” even opposite to â€” predictive staleness (stale-but-still-reconstructable data can have a longer or shorter protected term than its relevance would imply). Indexing an economic TERM to a monotonically DRIFTING reconstruction bound â€” durability = f(R(t)) â€” is the unclaimed move; it converts an information-theoretic non-reconstruction quantity into the maturity date of subject-owned capital, which none of the valuation, propertization, or privacy-metric literatures do.
